before.content_html:
Energy Stores and Transfers

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between different energy stores. Scientists recognise eight main stores: chemical, nuclear, kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, electrostatic and electromagnetic. When energy is transferred from one store to another, it is moved by processes called working (for example, by an electric current or a force) or heating.

Electricity is a particularly convenient way to transfer energy. Chemical energy stored in a fuel or battery is converted to electrical energy, which can then be transmitted over large distances and converted into other useful forms — thermal energy in a heater, kinetic energy in a motor, or light in a lamp.

Power and Energy Transfer

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. It is measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 joule per second. A 2 kW kettle transfers twice as much energy per second as a 1 kW toaster. The energy transferred by any electrical appliance depends on both its power rating and the time for which it is used:

$$E = P \times t$$

where \(E\) is energy in joules (or kilowatt-hours), \(P\) is power in watts (or kilowatts) and \(t\) is time in seconds (or hours).

Key Fact

Energy transferred = power × time. In SI units: joules = watts × seconds. In everyday units: kilowatt-hours (kWh) = kilowatts × hours. A device with a power rating of 2 kW running for 3 hours transfers 6 kWh of energy.

Efficiency and Dissipation

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient. Some energy is always dissipated — it spreads into the surroundings as thermal energy and becomes increasingly difficult to make use of. A light bulb converts electrical energy into useful light and wasted thermal energy; a car engine converts chemical energy into useful kinetic energy and wasted thermal energy.

Efficiency is the fraction of total energy input that is converted into a useful output:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy transferred (J)}}{\text{total energy transferred (J)}}$$

An efficiency of 0.75 means 75% of the input energy becomes useful energy; the remaining 25% is dissipated. Ways to increase efficiency include lubrication (reducing friction in motors) and thermal insulation (slowing heat loss from buildings).

Question: An electric motor receives 500 J of electrical energy and produces 375 J of useful kinetic energy. Calculate its efficiency.

Step 1 — identify the equation: efficiency = useful energy ÷ total energy

Step 2 — substitute values: efficiency = 375 ÷ 500

Step 3 — calculate: efficiency = 0.75 (or 75%)

This means 75 J in every 100 J of electrical input becomes useful kinetic energy; 25 J is dissipated as thermal energy.

Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources

The main renewable energy sources include wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal and biofuels. They produce little or no carbon dioxide in use and will not run out. Non-renewable sources — fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) and nuclear fuel — provide reliable on-demand power but fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to global warming, and nuclear fuel produces radioactive waste.

Key Fact

Renewable sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, biofuel) do not run out and produce little CO2 in use. Non-renewable sources (coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear) provide reliable generation but fossil fuels produce CO2 and nuclear fuel creates radioactive waste.

In most power stations, a generator produces electricity by spinning a magnet near a coil of wire. The fuel source (fossil fuel, nuclear, or a renewable source) is used to drive the turbine that turns the generator. The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at 50 Hz and approximately 230 volts.

Electricity is distributed across the country through the National Grid at very high voltages. High voltage reduces the current for a given power, which reduces energy losses in the cables (because power dissipated in a wire depends on the square of the current). Transformers step up the voltage for transmission and step it back down for domestic use. Most home appliances are connected by a three-core cable containing live, neutral and earth wires.

Decisions About Energy Sources

Choices about energy sources involve weighing up scientific evidence, environmental impact, reliability, cost and social factors. Different people in different contexts may come to different conclusions about which sources to prioritise — a country with strong winds may favour offshore wind differently from one with high solar irradiance. These decisions are shaped by risk-benefit analysis and are ultimately a matter of policy, informed by but not determined solely by science.

Building Insulation and Reducing Energy Loss

One of the most cost-effective ways to reduce energy consumption is to reduce the energy lost from buildings. Heat loss through walls, roofs and windows is determined by the thickness and thermal conductivity of the materials used. A thicker wall slows heat transfer; a wall made of a material with low thermal conductivity (such as foam insulation) slows it further. Double-glazing traps a layer of air or gas between two panes of glass: air is a poor thermal conductor, so heat transfer across the window is significantly reduced.

Sankey diagrams are a useful tool for visualising energy transfers. In a Sankey diagram, the width of the arrows is proportional to the amount of energy they represent. The main arrow shows the total energy input; branches show where useful energy goes and where energy is wasted (dissipated). Reading a Sankey diagram allows you to estimate efficiency quickly: a diagram where the useful output arrow is wide relative to the wasted energy arrows indicates a more efficient device.

practice_questions.text: A 1500 W hair dryer is used for 4 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred by the hair dryer. Give your answer in joules.
practice_questions.marks: Convert time: 4 minutes = 240 s [1]. \(E = P \times t = 1500 \times 240 = 360\,000\) J (360 kJ) [1].

practice_questions.text: An electric motor receives 800 J of electrical energy and transfers 600 J as useful kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency of the motor and state what happens to the remaining energy.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 600 ÷ 800 = 0.75 (75%) [1+1 for correct substitution and answer]. The remaining 200 J (25%) is dissipated [1] as thermal energy to the surroundings [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable energy source. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Renewable: can be replenished within a human timescale / will not run out [1]; example such as wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal or biofuel [1]. Non-renewable: cannot be replenished within a human timescale [1]; example such as coal, oil, gas or nuclear fuel [1]. (Any two marks from four bullet points.)

practice_questions.text: Compare the environmental impacts of generating electricity using fossil fuels and using wind turbines.
practice_questions.marks: Fossil fuels: release carbon dioxide when burned [1]; this contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming [1]. Wind turbines: produce no carbon dioxide during generation [1]; but visual impact on landscape, potential noise, and effects on local wildlife are concerns [1]. (Accept other valid environmental comparisons.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity from power stations is transmitted at high voltage through the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks: Transmitting at high voltage reduces the current needed to transfer the same power [1]. Lower current means less energy is dissipated as thermal energy in the cables (energy losses are lower) [1]. This makes transmission more efficient over long distances [1].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of nuclear power as an energy source for generating electricity. Consider both the advantages and the disadvantages in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that nuclear power is a non-renewable but low-CO2 source; explains that it provides reliable, on-demand generation unlike intermittent renewables; discusses the risks including radioactive waste (long-lived, difficult to dispose of) and potential for serious accidents; considers economic factors (high construction cost, long build time); weighs advantages against disadvantages and reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Gives at least two clear advantages and two disadvantages with brief explanation; attempts a conclusion.
Developing: Lists some advantages and disadvantages without clearly weighing them.
Emerging: Makes one or two simple points without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a plastic rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed with a cloth.
practice_questions.marks: Electrons are transferred from the cloth to the plastic rod [1]. The rod gains extra electrons, giving it a net negative charge [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the forces between two negatively charged objects and between a negatively charged object and a positively charged object.
practice_questions.marks: Two negatively charged objects repel each other [1]. A negatively charged object and a positively charged object attract each other [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by an electric field and how it explains the force between two charged objects that are not touching.
practice_questions.marks: An electric field is a region of space around a charged object [1]. Any other charged object that enters the field experiences a force [1]. This force acts without the objects needing to touch, because the field occupies the space between them [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a spark is produced when a person who has built up static charge touches a metal door handle.
practice_questions.marks: Static charge builds up on the person (by friction between clothing/shoes and the floor) [1]. When they touch the metal handle, the charge difference is large enough for the electric field to ionise the air between finger and handle [1]. Charge flows rapidly through the ionised air, producing a spark [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why static electricity builds up on insulating materials but not on conducting materials.
practice_questions.marks: Electrons transferred by rubbing can move freely through a conductor [1]. In a conductor the charge would quickly flow away to earth rather than building up [1]. In an insulator, electrons cannot move freely, so transferred charge remains at the point of transfer and builds up [1].

practice_questions.text: A student rubs a polythene rod with a wool cloth. Describe what happens to the rod and the cloth in terms of electron transfer, and predict what will happen when the rod is brought close to another polythene rod that has been similarly charged.
practice_questions.marks: Electrons are transferred from the wool cloth to the polythene rod [1]; the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth becomes positively charged [1]. A second similarly treated rod also becomes negatively charged [1]. Two negatively charged objects repel each other, so the rods will push apart / repel [1].

practice_questions.text: A resistor has a potential difference of 6 V across it and a current of 2 A flowing through it. Calculate its resistance.
Two resistors of 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series with a 12 V supply. Calculate (a) the total resistance, (b) the current through the circuit, (c) the potential difference across the 5 Ω resistor.
practice_questions.marks: (a) \(R_{\text{total}} = 3 + 5 = 8\) Ω [1]. (b) \(I = V / R = 12 / 8 = 1.5\) A [1]. (c) \(V = I \times R = 1.5 \times 5 = 7.5\) V [1]. (Check: PD across 3 Ω = 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 V; 7.5 + 4.5 = 12 V ✓ — award this mark for correct working even without explicit check) [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a series circuit and a parallel circuit in terms of current and potential difference.
practice_questions.marks: Series: current is the same through every component [1]; potential difference is shared between components in proportion to their resistance [1]. Parallel: the same potential difference appears across every branch [1]; current splits between branches, more flowing through branches of lower resistance [1].

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'In a series circuit, the current gets smaller after passing through a resistor.' Explain why this statement is incorrect.
practice_questions.marks: Current is not used up as it passes through a component [1]. Charge flows continuously in a loop and the current (rate of flow of charge) is the same at every point in a series circuit [1]. What decreases across a resistor is the potential difference (voltage), not the current — energy is transferred to the resistor [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would investigate the I-V characteristics of a resistor in the laboratory. Identify the independent, dependent and control variables.
practice_questions.marks: Connect the resistor in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor (rheostat) and in parallel with a voltmeter [1]. Vary the voltage using the rheostat (independent variable: potential difference) [1]; record current from the ammeter (dependent variable: current) [1]; control variables include the resistor used and room temperature; plot I against V and check for a straight line through the origin [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference in resistance behaviour between a thermistor and a fixed resistor as temperature increases.
practice_questions.marks: A fixed resistor has a constant resistance that does not change with temperature [1]. A thermistor is a non-ohmic component whose resistance decreases as temperature increases [1]. This is because at higher temperatures more charge carriers (electrons) are available to conduct, reducing resistance [1].

before.exam_tip_html: The most heavily examined mistake in circuits is claiming that current is smaller after passing through a component in a series circuit. Current does not get used up — it is the same everywhere in a series loop. Only potential difference changes across components. Make sure you also understand the contrast between series and parallel: in series, total resistance increases as you add components; in parallel, total resistance decreases. For I-V graph questions, describe the shape carefully: a straight line through the origin = ohmic; a curve = non-ohmic. State the reason for the curve (e.g. filament gets hotter so resistance increases). For calculation questions, always show your working and include units.

before.content_html:
Mains Electricity in the UK

The electricity supplied to UK homes and schools is alternating current (a.c.). It operates at approximately 230 V and changes direction 50 times per second — a frequency of 50 Hz. This is quite different from the direct current (d.c.) you get from a battery, which always flows the same way.

Key Fact

UK mains electricity: approximately 230 V, alternating current (a.c.), 50 Hz frequency. Batteries and cells supply direct current (d.c.).

The Three-Pin Plug

Most mains appliances connect to the supply via a three-pin plug. Understanding the role of each wire is essential for electrical safety.

Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the mains supply. It alternates between positive and negative peaks.

Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit and is kept close to 0 V (earth potential).

Earth wire (green and yellow stripes) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. If a fault causes the casing to become live, the earth wire carries the current safely to ground, blowing the fuse and breaking the circuit.

Even with an appliance switched off, the live wire remains at mains voltage relative to earth. If someone touches it, there is a large potential difference between their hand and the ground, which drives a current through the body. This is why switches must always be wired into the live wire — breaking the live side ensures no voltage reaches the appliance.

Fuses and Circuit Breakers

A fuse is wired into the live wire. If a fault causes excessive current to flow, the fuse wire heats up and melts, breaking the circuit before the appliance or cable can overheat and catch fire. Fuses are rated in amps (e.g. 3 A, 5 A, 13 A) — the correct fuse rating is just above the normal operating current of the appliance.

Key Fact

A circuit breaker performs the same protective function as a fuse but can be reset by flicking a switch. This makes circuit breakers more convenient — but both devices must be positioned in the live wire to be effective.

Electrical Power

The power of an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers every second. Two equations link power to current and potential difference:

$$P = IV$$

$$P = I^2 R$$

where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(I\) is current in amps (A), \(V\) is potential difference in volts (V), and \(R\) is resistance in ohms (\(\Omega\)).

A hairdryer is rated at 1150 W and operates on a 230 V mains supply. Calculate the current it draws and select the correct fuse.

Rearrange \(P = IV\): \(I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{1150}{230} = 5\) A

Since the normal current is 5 A, a 5 A fuse would blow under normal use. Select a 13 A fuse — the next standard rating above 5 A — to protect the cable while allowing normal operation.

Energy Transferred in a Circuit

The energy an appliance transfers depends on its power and how long it runs:

$$E = Pt$$

where \(E\) is energy in joules (J), \(P\) is power in watts (W), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). You can also calculate energy transferred using charge: \(E = QV\), where \(Q\) is the charge in coulombs (C) that has flowed and \(V\) is the potential difference across the component.

A 60 W lamp is left on for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred.

Convert time to seconds: \(t = 2 \times 3600 = 7200\) s

\(E = Pt = 60 \times 7200 = 432{,}000\) J = 432 kJ

Using the charge equation: if the current is \(I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{60}{230} \approx 0.26\) A, then charge \(Q = It = 0.26 \times 7200 \approx 1872\) C. Check: \(E = QV = 1872 \times 230 \approx 430{,}560\) J ✓ (rounding difference).

Transformers and the National Grid

The National Grid transmits electricity at very high voltages (hundreds of thousands of volts) and correspondingly low currents. The reason: power lost as heat in the cables equals \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\). A smaller current means far less wasted energy in the resistance of the cables.

A transformer changes the voltage of an a.c. supply. A step-up transformer at the power station increases voltage (and reduces current) before transmission. Step-down transformers near homes reduce the voltage back to a safe 230 V for domestic use.

Because energy is conserved in an ideal transformer, the power in equals the power out: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). This is why stepping up voltage forces the current to decrease proportionally.

practice_questions.text: State the voltage and frequency of the UK mains electricity supply, and identify whether it is alternating or direct current.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: approximately 230 V, alternating current (a.c.)
1 mark: frequency of 50 Hz

Emerging: states voltage only or describes as a.c. without frequency.
Developing: states voltage and a.c. but omits frequency, or gives frequency without voltage.
Secure: correctly states ~230 V, a.c., 50 Hz.

practice_questions.text: A laptop charger is rated at 45 W and plugged into the 230 V mains. Calculate the current drawn by the charger.
practice_questions.marks:
\(I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{45}{230} = 0.196\) A (accept 0.20 A)

1 mark for correct rearrangement and substitution.
1 mark for correct answer with unit (A).

Common error: dividing V by P instead of P by V.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the live wire in a mains plug is dangerous even when the appliance is switched off.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states the live wire is at high voltage.
Secure: explains the live wire is at mains voltage (approximately 230 V) relative to earth, even with the switch open, because the switch breaks the circuit on the appliance side not the supply side.
Mastering: extends to explain that touching the live wire creates a potential difference between the person and earth, driving a current through the body, which can cause serious injury.

[1 mark: live wire remains at mains voltage/potential difference relative to earth; 1 mark: switch is on the appliance side so does not disconnect the live wire from supply; 1 mark: touching live wire causes current to flow through the body to earth]

practice_questions.text:
A 2.5 kW electric heater is used for 90 minutes.
(a) Calculate the energy transferred in joules.
(b) Calculate the charge that flows if the heater operates at 230 V.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Convert: 2.5 kW = 2500 W; 90 min = 5400 s
\(E = Pt = 2500 \times 5400 = 13{,}500{,}000\) J (13.5 MJ) [2 marks: 1 for correct conversion, 1 for final answer with unit]

(b) \(Q = \frac{E}{V} = \frac{13{,}500{,}000}{230} \approx 58{,}696\) C (accept 58{,}700 C) [2 marks: 1 for correct equation/substitution, 1 for answer with unit C]

Common error: failing to convert kW to W or minutes to seconds.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the equation for power loss in cables (\(P = I^2 R\)), why the National Grid transmits electrical energy at high voltage rather than low voltage.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states that high voltage means low current.
Secure: uses \(P = IV\) to explain that for the same power, increasing voltage requires a smaller current, and then applies \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\) to show that less current means less power lost as heat.
Mastering: fully chains the argument — power transmitted is constant; step-up transformer increases voltage, so current decreases proportionally; since power loss \(= I^2 R\), squaring the smaller current gives a much smaller loss, making high-voltage transmission significantly more efficient.

[1 mark: high voltage → lower current for same power; 1 mark: power loss = I²R, so lower current means less heat loss in cables; 1 mark: links to transformer action stepping up voltage at the generating station]

practice_questions.text:
A student tests three appliances and records their power ratings: a lamp (100 W), a kettle (2200 W) and a phone charger (10 W). All operate at 230 V.
Select the correct fuse rating (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) for the kettle and justify your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: selects 13 A fuse without calculation.
Developing: calculates current \(I = P/V = 2200/230 \approx 9.6\) A and selects 13 A, but explanation is limited.
Secure: calculates \(I \approx 9.6\) A; explains the fuse must be rated just above the normal operating current, so 13 A is chosen (a 5 A fuse would blow under normal use; a 13 A fuse protects against dangerous currents above ~13 A).
Mastering: as Secure, plus explains the fuse is in the live wire so it breaks the circuit before the cable can overheat; notes that using too high a rating defeats the purpose of the safety device; may contrast with the lamp (\(I \approx 0.43\) A → 3 A fuse) to show selection depends on appliance power.

[6 marks total: 2 for correct calculation and fuse selection; 2 for clear explanation of selection logic; 2 for explaining fuse purpose in context of safety]

before.exam_tip_html: For power and energy calculation questions, always write out the equation you are using and state the units at every step — examiners award marks for clear working. A common error is forgetting to convert minutes to seconds before using \(E = Pt\). When asked to choose a fuse rating, calculate the current from \(P = IV\), then select the fuse rated just above that value — not equal to it. For questions on the live wire, be precise: the live wire is dangerous because it is at a high potential difference relative to earth, not simply because it carries current.

before.content_html:
Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnetic material. The field is strongest at the poles and weakens with increasing distance. We represent magnetic fields with field lines — these lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet, and the closer together they are, the stronger the field.

Permanent magnets keep their magnetism at all times. Magnets made from iron, nickel, cobalt or steel can all attract magnetic materials. Induced magnets are materials that become temporarily magnetic when placed in an external field. Unlike permanent magnets, induced magnets are always attracted to the source of the field — they are never repelled.

Key Fact

Magnetic field lines run from north pole to south pole outside the magnet. The closer the lines, the stronger the field. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet — magnetic compasses align because the Earth has a magnetic core.

Electromagnetism

When an electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles around the conductor. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.

Winding the wire into a solenoid greatly strengthens the magnetic field because the fields of each turn add together inside the coil. The field pattern of a solenoid resembles that of a bar magnet, with a north end and a south end that depend on the direction of current flow. Placing a soft iron core inside the solenoid further increases the field strength, creating an electromagnet.

Electromagnets can be switched on and off, making them far more versatile than permanent magnets. The development of electromagnets during the 19th century had a transformative impact on society — enabling the electric telegraph (revolutionising long-distance communication), the electric bell, the relay switch, MRI scanners in hospitals, and cranes in scrapyards that lift and release steel on demand. This is a clear example of how a scientific discovery leads to technological changes that improve people's lives.

In loudspeakers and headphones, a current-carrying coil is placed inside the field of a permanent magnet. The solenoid generates a magnetic field that interacts with the permanent magnet's field; varying the current in the coil causes the coil to vibrate at the corresponding frequency, pushing a cone to create sound waves that match the original electrical signal.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying conductor is placed inside a magnetic field, the conductor experiences a force — this is called the motor effect. The interaction between the magnetic field of the conductor and the external magnetic field creates a force on the wire. The force is greatest when the current is perpendicular to the field, and zero when they are parallel. Reversing either the current direction or the field direction reverses the force direction.

Key Fact

Fleming's left-hand rule: hold the left hand with the thumb, first finger and second finger at right angles to each other. The First finger points in the direction of the Field (north to south); the seCond finger points in the direction of Conventional current; the thuMb shows the direction of Motion (force). This rule shows the relative orientations of the force, the conductor and the magnetic field.

The size of the force can be calculated using:

$$F = BIl$$

where \(F\) is force in newtons (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is current in amps (A), and \(l\) is the length of conductor in the field in metres (m).

A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 4 A perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. Calculate the force on the wire.

\(F = BIl = 0.30 \times 4 \times 0.25 = 0.30\) N

The direction of the force would be found using Fleming's left-hand rule — the thumb indicates which way the wire is pushed.

The Electric Motor

A simple electric motor uses the motor effect to produce continuous rotation. A rectangular coil of wire is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows, the two sides of the coil that are parallel to the field axis experience opposite forces — one side is pushed up, the other down — creating a turning effect. As the coil rotates, this continuous force produces sustained rotation, converting electrical energy into kinetic energy.

Electromagnetic Induction and Generators

If a conducting wire moves through a magnetic field — or if the magnetic field around a stationary wire changes — a potential difference is induced across the wire's ends. This is electromagnetic induction. If the circuit is complete, a current will flow.

The direction of the induced potential difference is such that it drives a current which would create a magnetic field opposing the original change — this is a consequence of energy conservation.

In a generator, a magnet or electromagnet is rotated inside a coil of wire. As the magnet rotates, the magnetic field through the coil continuously changes, inducing a potential difference. This produces an alternating current (a.c.) — the voltage reverses direction once per revolution of the magnet.

A transformer works by induction: alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which induces an alternating potential difference in the secondary coil. The ratio of voltages equals the ratio of turns:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$

Energy conservation means \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) — stepping up voltage reduces current, cutting heat losses in transmission cables (since \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\)). This discovery fundamentally changed how humanity generates and distributes power.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Magnetic field lines run from north to south outside a magnet; the closer the lines, the stronger the field. Electromagnets — solenoids with iron cores — can be switched on and off, enabling applications from MRI scanners to scrapyard cranes.
  • The motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction. Force \(F = BIl\) (Higher Tier).
  • Generators convert kinetic energy to electrical energy by rotating a magnet in a coil (electromagnetic induction). Transformers change a.c. voltage using the ratio of turns on each coil, enabling efficient long-distance power transmission.
before.exam_tip_html: For questions on the motor effect, always apply Fleming's left-hand rule carefully — set up all three fingers at right angles before reading off the direction. A common error is using the right hand (which is for generators). For \(F = BIl\), the length \(l\) is only the length of conductor inside the magnetic field, not the total wire length. For extended-response questions on the impact of electromagnetism, include a named example (e.g. MRI scanners, electric motors in trains) and explain the mechanism, not just the application.

knowledge_checks.q: Which hand does Fleming's left-hand rule apply to when finding the direction of force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
options: It depends on the current direction

knowledge_checks.q: What type of current does an a.c. generator produce?
options: Direct current — it always flows the same way
Alternating current — it reverses direction periodically
Pulsating current — it switches on and off
Zero current — a generator stores energy

An induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed inside an external _____, and loses its magnetism when removed.
Match each component to its function:

Changes the voltage of an a.c. supply using electromagnetic induction
A solenoid with a soft iron core that can be switched on and off

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field at all times / retains its magnetism permanently.
1 mark: an induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed in an external field and loses its magnetism when the field is removed.

Note: induced magnets are always attracted to the source — never repelled.

practice_questions.text: A current-carrying wire of length 0.40 m is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. The current in the wire is 3.0 A. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice_questions.marks:
\(F = BIl = 0.25 \times 3.0 \times 0.40 = 0.30\) N

1 mark for correct substitution into \(F = BIl\).
1 mark for correct answer with unit (N).

Common error: using total wire length rather than only the length inside the field.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you could demonstrate that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field. State what equipment you would use and what you would observe.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states using a compass near a wire.
Secure: places a plotting compass near a straight wire carrying a current; observes that the compass needle deflects when current flows and returns to its original position when current is switched off; reversing the current reverses the needle deflection.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that the field lines form concentric circles around the wire, and increasing the current produces a greater deflection (stronger field).

[1 mark: compass near current-carrying wire; 1 mark: needle deflects when current flows / returns when current off; 1 mark: reversing current reverses deflection / field lines are concentric circles]

practice_questions.text:
A simple a.c. generator consists of a rectangular coil rotating in a magnetic field.
(a) State one change to the generator that would increase the induced potential difference.
(b) Explain why the output from the generator is alternating rather than direct.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Any one of: rotate the coil faster; use a stronger magnet; increase the number of turns on the coil. [1 mark]

(b) As the coil rotates, the rate at which it cuts through the magnetic field lines changes continuously [1 mark]. When the coil is perpendicular to the field it cuts lines at the maximum rate, inducing maximum p.d.; when it is parallel to the field it cuts no lines and the induced p.d. is zero [1 mark]. Because the direction of cutting reverses each half-turn, the direction of the induced current reverses, producing a.c. [1 mark].

Emerging: states the output reverses without explanation.
Mastering: links to the rate of change of flux explicitly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of practical electric motors has made a significant positive difference to people's lives. Give two specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: names one or two uses of electric motors without explaining the benefit.
Secure: names two applications (e.g. electric trains / trams reduce air pollution in cities; electric motors in medical equipment such as ventilators keep patients alive); explains the mechanism of the motor effect in each context (rotating coil in magnetic field).
Mastering: as Secure, plus evaluates whether the benefits outweigh any downsides (e.g. electricity must still be generated; rare earth materials needed for magnets); acknowledges that the impact was not immediately obvious when electromagnetic induction was first discovered.

[1 mark: named application 1 with benefit explained; 1 mark: named application 2 with benefit explained; 1 mark: motor mechanism linked to application; 1 mark: evaluation of impact/limitation; 1 mark: reference to how technology developed from scientific discovery]

practice_questions.text:
A transformer has 500 turns on its primary coil and 2500 turns on its secondary coil. The primary p.d. is 230 V and the primary current is 10 A.
(a) Calculate the secondary p.d.
(b) Calculate the secondary current, assuming the transformer is ideal.
(c) Explain why a step-up transformer is used at power stations before electricity is transmitted through the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\) → \(V_s = \frac{230 \times 2500}{500} = 1150\) V [2 marks: 1 for correct equation, 1 for answer]

(b) \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) → \(I_s = \frac{230 \times 10}{1150} = 2\) A [1 mark]

(c) Stepping up voltage to a high value reduces the current (\(P = IV\) — same power, higher V means lower I). Lower current reduces heat lost in cables (\(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\)), making long-distance transmission far more efficient. [2 marks: 1 for lower current argument; 1 for linking to \(I^2 R\) heat loss reduction]

Emerging: only states high voltage is used.
Mastering: chains the full argument — transformer equation → lower current → \(I^2 R\) loss reduction → more energy reaches consumers. [1 mark for clear logical chain]
